notes.headline: Nebius: revenue up 571% to $981 million and a $466 million EBITDA profit, but data-centre delays and a $27 billion spending plan sink the shares
notes.takeaway: Revenue jumped 571% to $980.8 million, above estimates, and adjusted EBITDA swung to a $465.8 million profit. But delays at partner data centres pushed some revenue into 2027, 2026 revenue guidance was trimmed to $3.0–$3.2 billion, and capital spending plans rose to $27 billion this year and $40–$45 billion next. The shares fell 17% on the day and kept falling.
results: Nebius Group reported revenue of $980.8 million for the third quarter, up from $146.1 million a year earlier and up 68% from the second quarter. Adjusted EBITDA was $465.8 million against a $5.2 million loss, and adjusted net income $90.9 million against a $100.4 million loss. The net loss from continuing operations narrowed to $37.5 million from $119.6 million.

Operating costs rose to $930.4 million but fell to 95% of revenue from 189%. Depreciation, the largest single cost for a company renting out GPUs, rose 258% to $354.7 million. Cost of revenue fell to 22% of sales from 29%.

Capital spending was $7.3 billion in the quarter and $15.4 billion over nine months. Nine-month operating cash flow was $4.2 billion, driven by customer prepayments, which the company said covered more than 100% of the capital spending tied to deals signed in the quarter. Nebius also raised $5.75 billion of debt during the quarter.
mgmt: Founder and chief executive Arkady Volozh published his quarterly shareholder letter alongside the results. According to the company’s guidance as reported by news outlets, delays at third-party data-centre sites will push some capacity — and some revenue expected for December — into early 2027, so full-year 2026 revenue is now expected at $3.0 to $3.2 billion, against a previous range of $3.0 to $3.4 billion.

Nebius raised its 2026 capital spending guidance to about $27 billion from $20 to $25 billion and introduced a 2027 outlook of $12 to $13 billion of revenue with $40 to $45 billion of capital spending, well above analysts’ expectations for spending.
view: Nebius is one of the purest bets on the AI infrastructure boom: it builds data centres packed with Nvidia GPUs and rents them to AI labs and large technology companies, including multi-billion-dollar contracts with Microsoft and Meta. The quarter itself was extraordinary — revenue up more than six-fold and a 47% EBITDA margin. The stock fell because investors are no longer judging these companies on revenue growth but on the cost and timing of the capacity needed to deliver it.

The numbers explain the concern. Guiding to $12–$13 billion of revenue next year while spending $40–$45 billion means Nebius will invest more than three dollars for every dollar of revenue, funded by prepayments, debt and potentially new shares. That works only if the contracts hold, the GPUs stay productive long enough to earn back their cost, and the data centres arrive on time — and this quarter showed the last condition is already slipping. Prepayments covering the spending tied to new deals is a genuine positive, because it means customers are financing much of the build-out, but it does not cover the older capacity or the larger 2027 plan.

After a fall of nearly 50% from its peak this month, the shares now price significant execution risk. The bull case is that Nebius has contracted demand from the deepest-pocketed buyers in the world and is turning profitable at the EBITDA level faster than expected. The bear case is that it is a capital-hungry landlord in a market where GPU prices may fall, competition from CoreWeave and the hyperscalers is intense, and any delay compounds the funding need. Investors should watch financing as closely as revenue.
notes.watch: Watch delivery dates for the delayed data-centre sites, how the 2027 spending is financed (debt, prepayments or new shares), revenue concentration among the largest customers, and GPU rental pricing.
